text: Scaled dot‑product attention takes a set of query vectors, computes their dot products with all key vectors, divides each dot product by √d_k, and then applies a softmax to obtain weights for the values [S1]. The output for each query is a weighted sum of the values, where the weights indicate how well the query matches each key [S1]. Dividing by √d_k prevents the dot products from growing too large when d_k is large, which would push the softmax into regions with very small gradients [S1]. This scaling stabilizes training and keeps the attention computation efficient for high‑dimensional representations [S1].
raw_drafts: Scaled dot‑product attention takes a set of query vectors and compares each query to all key vectors by computing their dot products, then uses a softmax to turn these scores into weights for a weighted sum of the corresponding value vectors. The output for each query is therefore a weighted combination of the values, where the weights reflect how well the query matches each key. In practice the dot products are divided by \(\sqrt{d_k}\) before the softmax \([S1]\). This scaling keeps the dot‑product magnitudes from growing with the dimensionality \(d_k\), which would otherwise push the softmax into very steep regions with tiny gradients, making learning harder \([S1]\). The division therefore stabilizes training and allows dot‑product attention to work efficiently even for large feature dimensions.

Multi‑head attention lets the model jointly attend to information from different representation sub‑spaces at different positions, whereas a single head would average these signals and inhibit such specialization【S1】.  
The Transformer therefore splits the 512‑dimensional model into 8 parallel heads, each using a 64‑dimensional key, value and query projection (d_k = d_v = d_model/h = 64)【S1】.  
These 8 heads are concatenated and linearly projected to produce the final output, keeping the overall computational cost comparable to a single‑head full‑dimensional attention【S1】.

The authors argue that multiple heads let the model jointly attend to information from different representation sub‑spaces at different positions; with a single head the averaging of these sub‑spaces would inhibit this diversity [S1]. Multi‑head attention therefore improves the ability to capture varied patterns such as long‑range dependencies and syntactic relations [S1]. In the paper the authors use \(h = 8\) parallel heads, each projecting to a key, query and value dimension of \(d_k = d_v = d_{\text{model}}/h = 64\) [S1]. The overall model dimensionality is \(d_{\text{model}} = 512\), so each head works in a 64‑dimensional space while the concatenated output remains 512‑dimensional [S4][S1]. The total computational cost of this multi‑head setup is comparable to that of a single‑head attention with full dimensionality because the per‑head dimensions are reduced [S1]. Thus, several heads are employed to capture diverse attention patterns, with the configuration \(h = 8,\ d_k = d_v = 64\) in a 512‑dimensional model.

text: Positional encodings are added to token embeddings so that the model can use order information; they have the same dimension \(d_{\text{model}}\) as the embeddings so they can be summed [S1]. Each dimension of the encoding is a sinusoid, defined as \(\text{PE}_{\text{pos},2i}= \sin(\text{pos}/10000^{2i/d_{\text{model}}})\) and \(\text{PE}_{\text{pos},2i+1}= \cos(\text{pos}/10000^{2i/d_{\text{model}}})\), where the wavelengths form a geometric progression from \(2\pi\) to \(10000\cdot 2\pi\) [S1]. The authors chose this form because a fixed offset \(k\) can be represented as a linear function of the positional encoding, which should make it easier to learn relative position attention and may allow the model to extrapolate to longer sequences than seen during training [S1]. They also experimented with learned positional embeddings and found that performance was nearly identical to the sinusoidal version, but favored the sinusoidal form for its extrapolation property [S2]. Thus, sinusoids are built by summing sine and cosine functions of geometrically spaced frequencies and are preferred over learned embeddings primarily for their theoretical ability to represent relative positions and generalize to unseen sequence lengths [S1][S2].

The minimum number of sequential operations required by a self‑attention layer is a constant \(O(1)\), in contrast to the linear‑time \(O(n)\) sequential operations of a recurrent layer [S2]. Regarding path length, a self‑attention layer connects every pair of positions directly, giving a maximum path length of \(O(1)\) [S2]. text: Traditional spoken dialogue systems struggle to feel natural because their multi‑component pipelines introduce several latencies that accumulate to several seconds, far longer than the few hundred‑millisecond response times of real conversations [S2]. In addition, these systems rely on text as an intermediate modality, which discards non‑linguistic cues such as emotion, accent, and background sounds that are essential for natural speech perception and meaning [S2]. Finally, the turn‑based design of current models assumes clean, speaker‑separated segments, ignoring overlapping speech, interruptions, and backchanneling that constitute 10–20 % of spoken time in natural dialogue [S2]. These limitations together make the overall experience feel artificial and unnatural to users [S1][S2].

text: Moshi is full‑duplex because its architecture is explicitly built as a multi‑stream speech‑to‑speech Transformer that processes the user’s audio and Moshi’s own output audio in parallel, eliminating the need for explicit speaker‑turn boundaries and allowing each side to speak at any moment [S4][S2]. The model jointly generates semantic and acoustic tokens for both streams in a hierarchical, streaming fashion, so that as soon as a user utterance starts, Moshi can start producing its response while still listening to the user [S4]. Inner Monologue further enables this by predicting time‑aligned text tokens as a prefix to audio tokens, which provides linguistic grounding without blocking real‑time audio generation [S1][S5]. Thus, Moshi handles simultaneous speech by maintaining two concurrent token streams—one for the user and one for itself—within the same Transformer, allowing overlapping speech and interruptions to be modeled naturally [S2][S4].

text: Inner Monologue is a hierarchical modeling component of Moshi that predicts a structured sequence of text, semantic, and acoustic tokens in a single generative framework, allowing all utterances to be represented as both text and speech while remaining compatible with streaming inference [S5][S4]. It decomposes speech on a per‑frame basis, outputting a speech frame at each prediction step, which contrasts with models that first generate a complete text sequence before producing audio tokens, thereby enabling real‑time generation [S2]. By introducing a controllable delay between the text sequence (W_t) and the audio tokens (A_t,q), the model can decide whether the audio is conditioned on previously generated text (TTS) or whether the text is conditioned on previously listened audio (ASR) [S3]. In a streaming TTS configuration, the text is advanced ahead of the audio so that sampled audio tokens are dictated by the preceding text tokens; in a streaming ASR configuration, audio tokens are advanced ahead of the text, allowing the model to listen before predicting text tokens, which at inference time is teacher‑forced with ground‑truth audio [S1]. The same architecture and training data can be switched between ASR and TTS simply by adjusting this single delay hyper‑parameter, without altering the loss, architecture, or training procedure [S1][S3]. Thus, Inner Monologue provides a unified framework that flexibly yields low‑latency streaming ASR and TTS by controlling the relative timing of text and audio token generation [S5].

raw_drafts: H‑Net learns where to cut the byte stream by training a **routing module** that predicts a binary boundary indicator for each input byte, using both the local byte content and the surrounding contextual representation that has been built by the preceding layers of the network. The module is end‑to‑end differentiable, so its parameters are optimized jointly with the main backbone via standard gradient descent. In practice, the learned segmentation tends to place boundaries at “spacelike” bytes (e.g., whitespace characters) and at the first few characters of each word, mirroring natural delimiters that the model discovers on its own, while also merging multiple words into larger chunks when the surrounding context suggests a higher‑level semantic unit [S4]. This content‑ and context‑aware chunking is hierarchical: the first stage focuses on low‑level delimiters and word onsets, and subsequent stages combine these into increasingly abstract units such as whole words or phrases, all without any external heuristics or supervision [S4]. The routing decisions are therefore data‑dependent and learned directly from the optimization objective of the language model, allowing H‑Net to compress the input sequence to a resolution comparable to BPE tokenizers while preserving semantically salient positions [S1].

H‑Net decides where to cut the byte stream with a learned **routing module** that outputs a binary boundary indicator for each byte in the sequence, using both local and contextual information to guide the decision [S1]. The routing module is part of the dynamic chunking (DC) mechanism, which compresses the raw input by selectively retaining vectors at positions marked as boundaries while discarding others [S1]. Because the routing module is differentiable via a straight‑through estimator, its parameters are optimized jointly with the rest of the backbone through standard gradient‑based training, allowing the segmentation strategy to evolve end‑to‑end without external supervision [S1]. Visualizations of H‑Net’s boundaries show that the module learns content‑ and context‑dependent patterns, such as placing cuts near whitespace or at the start of words, and even merging multiple words into a single chunk when the surrounding content suggests it [S4]. Thus, H‑Net dynamically determines chunk boundaries by predicting discrete boundary indicators that are trained together with the model’s representations.

[S1] 2410.00037v1 p.24 §5.2: "In consequence, Mimi proves to be a well-fitted audio tokenizer to train real-time audio language models. A collateral finding of our study is a concerning lack of correlation between objective and subjective audio quality metrics. In particular, while we find VisQOL to provide a reliable proxy for perceived quality when modifying the generator architecture, changing the training objective (e.g. removing reconstruction losses) moves the score in directions that are completely decorrelated from human perception."
[S2] 2410.00037v1 pp.9-10 §3.3.1: "We discretize the latent space with a Residual Vector Quantizer (Zeghidour et al., 2022), which iteratively applies vector quantization (VQ) to the residuals of the previous quantizer. With Q quantizers, each with a codebook of N_A centroids, the R VQ discretizes the latent space into {1, . . . , N_A}^S×Q. As a baseline, we train this model with a combination of reconstruction and adversarial losses, following the setup of Encodec (Défossez et al., 2023). We detail below the main changes of Mimi with respect to this default configuration."
[S3] 2410.00037v1 p.23 §5.1: "For a fair comparison with SemantiCodec and SpeechTokenizer, we also include a downsampled version of our codec in the MUSHRA study. f_s is the audio sample rate and f_r the codec frame rate. Both Mimi codecs are trained with distillation, and either with the same combination of reconstruction and adversarial losses as Encodec (see Section 3.3) or adversarial losses only."
[S4] 2410.00037v1 pp.11-12 §3.3.2: "https://huggingface.co/microsoft/wavlm-large dimension of 1024, followed by average pooling with a stride of 4 and a kernel size of 8. Interestingly, we observed that it was critical for performance to perform this average pooling in a non-causal way, which is compatible with streaming inference as these embeddings are only used during training. We then compute a cosine distance between the output of the first quantizer and the transformed WavLM embeddings, to perform distillation. Table 3 shows that this distillation loss conflicts with reconstruction and adversarial losses targeting quality."
[S5] 2507.07955v2 p.8 §2.2.3: "Inspired by load balancing mechanisms in Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models (Fedus, Zoph, and Shazeer 2022), which face similar challenges in maintaining balanced expert utilization, we introduce a ratio loss to guide compression: L_ratio = N N− 1 ((N − 1)FG +(1−F)(1−G)), F = 1 L ∑︁^L t =1 b_t, G = 1 L ∑︁^L t =1 p_t, (10) whereF represents the fraction of vectors actually selected,G denotes the average boundary probability, andN controls the target compression ratio."
raw_drafts:
The ratio loss is a regulariser that steers a dynamic chunking module toward a user‑defined compression ratio. It is computed as  

\[
L_{\text{ratio}}=\frac{N}{N-1}\Big((N-1)F G+(1-F)(1-G)\Big)\,,
\]  

where the terms \(F\) and \(G\) are defined as  

\[
F=\frac{1}{L}\sum_{t=1}^{L} b_t,\quad G=\frac{1}{L}\sum_{t=1}^{L} p_t\,,
\]  

with \(b_t\) indicating whether a vector is kept and \(p_t\) being the model’s boundary probability for that vector. Thus \(F\) represents the fraction of vectors actually selected, while \(G\) is the average boundary probability. The hyper‑parameter \(N\) controls the target compression ratio: the loss is minimized when \(F=G=N^{-1}\), encouraging the module to retain the desired proportion of vectors. This loss is combined with an autoregressive prediction loss to maintain content‑adaptive compression while guiding the model toward the specified ratio. [S5]

The ratio loss is a regulariser that steers a dynamic chunking module toward a user‑defined compression ratio. It is defined as \(L_{\text{ratio}}=\frac{N}{N-1}\big((N-1)FG+(1-F)(1-G)\big)\) [S5]. In this expression, \(F\) represents the fraction of vectors actually selected during chunking [S5]. The term \(G\) denotes the average boundary probability, i.e., the average probability that a vector marks a chunk boundary [S5]. The hyper‑parameter \(N\) controls the target compression ratio; when \(F=G=N^{-1}\) the loss reaches its minimum of 1, guiding the model toward the desired compression level [S5].

text: In the experiments, a fixed‑width pooling variant of H‑Net (H‑Net (pool)) consistently underperformed all other H‑Net versions, demonstrating that static chunking is ineffective [S3]. By contrast, a single‑stage dynamic chunking model (H‑Net (1‑stage)) surpassed the static‑width variant and even the heuristic‑based SpaceByte, showing that context‑dependent segmentation improves performance [S3]. When dynamic chunking was applied recursively in a two‑stage hierarchy (H‑Net (2‑stage)), performance improved further, with the two‑stage model outperforming the one‑stage model across both Large and XL scales [S3]. The authors attribute this gain to the model’s ability to learn a nested hierarchy of useful features, leveraging compute and parameters more effectively with each additional stage [S3]. Overall, the results indicate that dynamic, learnable chunking—especially when iterated—provides a clear advantage over fixed‑width pooling for byte‑level sequence modeling [S4].
